utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. Good afternoon, everybody. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to introduce Mr. Avi Singh from my team who is assisting me here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Singh. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To begin today, I'd just like to go back very briefly to a couple of aspects of your evidence from yesterday, if I may. Yesterday I asked you at page 3093, lines 22 to 23, of the transcript of evidence whether the territory encompassed by the strategic objectives covered multi-ethnic areas. And your response was: "Yes, insofar as we can determine from the strategic objectives what was intended in territorial terms." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I went on then to say yes and give an example of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. Now, to follow-up on that in a way, could I ask you then whether the same applied to the fifth objective and the city of Sarajevo. Did the fifth objective also transect a multi-ethnic area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday when we broke we were talking about the ethnic distribution across Bosnia and Herzegovina and when we broke we were speaking about Sarajevo in particular in that regard. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you, going back to the first objective that you discussed yesterday of separation, the first overarching objective, could you tell us did it embrace any change to the country's ethnic distribution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the goal, if achieved, would certainly have -- would dramatically change the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- at least the ethnic distribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what regard? How so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have attached human residents to territoriality in a way that was radically different from the situation as of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the subject still of this overarching objective, was there any strategy that you see to achieving that objective, any central perhaps strategy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were strategies employed that actually well preceded the formal adoption of the strategic goals, and I divide those strategies into two, one being the -- a very public and -- I'd say public performance component of state building that the SDS leadership engaged in starting in October 1991 and proceeding for the next seven months in a series of steps taken in the Bosnian Serb Assembly and then a few cases outside of it. The second element is the -- what I call the municipal strategy, and that word is mine but I think it's apt to describe the SDS policies toward municipalities in the course of the period January 1991 through about the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask for a document be called up at this point in time, 65 ter 00972, which is a record of a speech by Dr. Karadzic on the occasion of the plebiscite of November 1991. And once we see that document I could ask you some further questions. Perhaps you could display the B/C/S page 2, which should be the first page of the document, and similarly English page 2. Could we go, please, to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours, I have not seen these two pages in the documents before. Thank you. And now on to page 4, please. I see two B/C/S pages in front of me rather than one English, one B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, given that you've indicated your -- you have command of the English and the Serbo-Croatian language, perhaps I could ask you this question with respect to the B/C/S version of the document, which is the cover page of the document. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a transcript of a speech that Dr. Karadzic delivered sometime in the days prior to the referendum of November 9 and 10, 1991. The two cover pages indicate that it was collected and transcribed by the state commission for the investigation of war crimes, I believe, which was headed by Mr. Gavran Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go now to page 9 of both versions, the English and B/C/S of this document, please. Now, on the English version, if I could direct your attention, please, Dr. Donia, to the very last paragraph, the sentence that begins immediately after the italicised portion of the last paragraph. And for the record, that same passage should be found at e-court, page 9 in B/C/S, nine lines up from the bottom of the page. Do you see the sentence, Dr. Donia, that begins: "Municipalities are not" -- and I'm sorry it's cut off on the left hand part of the English version. Thank you. "Municipalities are not God given ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this speech by Dr. Karadzic or this extract from Dr. Karadzic's speech then reads: "Municipalities are not God given. They were established to the disadvantage of the Serb people, in such a way that all Serb units in Bosnia were split and Serbs became a minority instead with their own municipality; let them also have a majority in their municipalities." Do you have any comment on this passage and this speech in any regard, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This passage essentially repeats the critique that I indicated yesterday developed by some Serb intellectuals in Bosnia, including Dr. Karadzic, in the last years of the 1980s and 1990, which argued that the municipal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was discriminatory against Serbs. The example of Ozren which Dr. Karadzic offers here, which he says he keeps repeating, he did indeed repeat on several occasions to argue that Ozren should have been its own municipality. Part of the rest of the speech goes on to spell out what he believes should be the remedy for that in terms of reorganising municipalities and laying claim to Serb land based on certain criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I offer this, please, as the next exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P958, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document that we've just looked at, Dr. Donia, is a very early-on document. Perhaps I could ask you, was there any -- was there any evolution to this municipal strategy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal strategy began very shortly after the elections of 1990 with a programme of regionalisation, and regionalisation at this point in time, which meant the first six, eight months of 1991, entailed taking existing municipalities and joining them together in community or associations of communities or communities of municipalities. The most significant and active of which was the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina, which was -- eventually had its seat in Banja Luka. The -- there was none or very little discussion at that point. There was certainly no effort to change existing municipal boundaries, but rather to associate these municipalities in a single body, an association of municipalities. A practice that had been followed under socialism as well, but established for the purpose of co-ordinating municipal services and other, let's say, points of convenience for the governance of these municipalities. The effort on the part of the SDS was a -- promoted by a single party with the intent of linking up the municipalities in which Serbs had an absolute or relative majority. That's the first phase of this and -- of the municipal strategy. It then was followed by a second phase in which the issue of revising municipal boundaries came to the forefront, and that can be identified as beginning in -- on October 15, 1991, one could pick other dates but that's the -- I think the operative date when the municipal strategy takes on this effort to try to alter municipal boundaries within the republic. And then a --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if I could just stop you at that moment. What happened on October 15, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 19 -- October 14th/15th is this watershed date in which the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a resolution called a declaration of sovereignty and a platform, which was a platform for the negotiating team for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be used in negotiations with the Europeans. And the point at which the SDS essentially lost the battle to veto the drive toward independence that the Croatian and the HDZ and the SDA, the Croatian and Muslim parties, had initiated. In the -- that happened in the very early morning hours of October 15th, and from that point on the energies of the SDS seem to have been directed largely toward planning a -- and it's not a single plan but a extended planning process which entailed a number of documents along the way and some shifting in tactics, but can be seen as a consistent planning process from that date into the early weeks of 19 -- or of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this point I'd like us to see a clip from a speech delivered by Dr. Karadzic at this Assembly session on October 15, 1991, that's 65 ter number 45005. And it should begin at timer number 00:07:56:3, and I hope that my colleagues -- the interpreters in the booth have received copies of the transcript. I'm sure I'll be advised if that's not the case. Could we begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not hearing any translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know if there's been a transcript that's been delivered. I thought we had taken steps to do that. It has been delivered. Perhaps we could be advised by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have a different transcript but not that one that you referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence then, for a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We've just received the proper copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hear that the proper copy has been delivered in the nick of time, and I apologise to my colleagues, the interpreters. And if it's possible, perhaps we could begin afresh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Sovereign people in Bosnia and Herzegovina can each say for themselves what they want but not for other people as well. It was one of the conclusions made in this Assembly. We shall disable you to carry out violence against Serbian people, constitution violence in front of local and international public. Because after the constitution violence, all other violence will come. We won't be consulted regarding the situation anymore. We won't be consulted if we come into the situation in which Slovenia and Croatia are in, especially Croatia. Knowing that in Bosnia and Herzegovina that hell would be 1.000 times worse and there would be no way to stop it. I must send a message to all delegates. Gentlemen, believe me, even if you would make -- if you were to make it because we have the constitutional manner to prevent you from voting, but even if you would make something that would be the source of shame for Mr. Izetbegovic in The Hague because we would have other ways to make it impossible, even in The Hague. It would also be a great shame for the image of this parliament in Europe, especially, you're embarrassing Croats and Muslims who are loyal to this idea. Your shame and your prove how much you respect sovereignty and equality of Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm asking you one more time. I'm not threatening, but asking, pleading, to take seriously the interpretation of the political will of the Serbian people which is represented here by the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian Movement of Renewal and several Serbs from other parties. Please take it seriously, it is not good what you are doing. This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people into possible extinction because Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here! "Please, I know these are serious words. Serious situations call for serious words. How will you prevent that everybody start killing everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Can war in Croatia be prevented? Especially in the border areas where Serbs and Croats are in contact, whose two political wills are in conflict, and weren't realised in a legal manner so there's only one way left to realise them. From now on gentlemen, I will ask for the floor on a regular basis until you take the matter of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina off the agenda. That is my right. I want to send a message to Muslim, Serb, and Croatian people that you want to achieve something in Europe what you have no right to. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my thanks to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you have any comment on what we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- this was a youthful and energetic Dr. Karadzic speaking to the Bosnian Serb Assembly -- or to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the multi-ethnic Assembly, in what was actually a fairly long address, the last part of which you have just played. And he seemed to gain momentum in the course of that speech and warned I think against taking the step of approving the two documents that I just cited. Said that he was not threatening but pleading, and then moved to a phase and used some expressions which at least were interpreted by others there as threats. That was language that he in fact had used in the weeks prior to that in telephone conversations with other SDS and Serb leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and we'll come back to those conversations you've just referred to in a short while.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But at this moment, Your Honour, I'd like to tender, if I may, the clip that's just been played from the timer number I originally cited 07:56:3 to 10:44:7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted -- oh, just a second. You have objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have something to add, and that is: Why don't you admit the entire speech? We will certainly be needing the entire speech, so why not admit it that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It seems quite practical, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long is the entire clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This -- your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My colleague's just raised an important point. If there's a difference between Dr. Karadzic's speech as a whole and the video as a whole and a significant time difference, and perhaps Dr. Karadzic could specify which portion he would like to see in that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we stick to our practice. So we'll admit this time only those part played at the courtroom, and then whether we can think about there can be a better way to admit these video-clips. This time only those played at the courtroom will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and we can take steps, of course, Your Honour, to see if there's any other portions which we can reach agreement on that might serve to help proceedings later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, you mentioned that the events of this day that we've just been discussing started a planning process as regards the municipal strategy. Was -- what was the next step after this date that you've been able to identify?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just say, I think they were followed by a planning process, not necessarily did they start it. But they were followed by a planning process which began with a meeting of the political counsel of the SDS, which was a group of largely academic advisors and other party -- leaders of the party. That convened on the evening of that same October 15th and discussed broadly and with no specific conclusions the options for party plans going forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And following that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the wake of that or in the aftermath of that meeting, the party leadership decided to take certain steps that had been discussed at that meeting in a particular order. They decided, first of all, to form a separate Assembly, to be made up of those members of the SDS and other parties -- other Serb parties that had been elected to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the November 1990 elections. They further decided to hold a plebiscite on a question which was essentially: Do you want to remain in Yugoslavia? To be held in early November. So their sequence was, first of all, to form the Bosnian Serb Assembly in October; then hold the plebiscite in November, the Bosnian Serb Assembly then ordering, organising, and managing the plebiscite. Following the plebiscite, other Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions were held. The December decision -- these came about once a month by coincidence, but the December decision was to announce preparations for the formation of a -- the Serbian -- Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then on January 8, to proclaim a separate state with that name. In February to approve a draft constitution. In March to implement that constitution or approve it, promulgate it. And then in April to formally declare the republic independent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to go back to my question, was there a next step to the municipal strategy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first the municipal strategy was kind of an integral part of the overall discussion. The -- many of the leaders favoured what they characterised as intensifying regionalisation, which meant essentially drawing -- redrawing municipal boundaries. At the third Bosnian Serb Assembly session on the 11th of December, the leaders of the party, specifically Mr. Krajisnik, supported by Dr. Karadzic, introduced a resolution which took this in a somewhat different direction, one that was not incompatible with redrawing municipal boundaries, but was given priority over it for the time being, and that was to create separate Serb Assemblies, Serbian Municipal Assemblies at the municipal level in those municipalities where Serbs lived. That resolution passed with one dissenting vote on the first try, and the chair, Mr. Krajisnik, evoked -- then asked the delegate who voted no why he had opposed it. And there followed then a discussion about the resolution itself and its relationship to the redrawing of municipal boundaries. And it became evident that there was considerable opposition in the Assembly to the idea of forming separate Serb Municipal Assemblies. Consequently, the bill was or the proposal was amended to make it voluntary, and then that voluntary recommendation passed unanimously. That was an Assembly session that was actually quite contentious, and in fact toward the very end of it Mr. Krajisnik adjourned -- abruptly adjourned the session and walked out of the hall. Then another leader stepped up and concluded the session. In the wake of that experience on the 11th of December, the municipal strategy took a new turn, and that was represented in the dissemination of a set of instructions to SDS municipal leaders that was dated the 19th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps at this juncture I can ask for 65 ter 00224 to be displayed, please. The cover page for that document should suffice in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in the meantime, Dr. Donia, so was that the resolution on 11th, the one you referred to as December decision in the previous answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the document that we're just now looking at was not disseminated until the 19th and was never voted on as a document by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, when you referred to December decision, so I didn't follow that -- okay, we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, do you see the pages in English and Serbo-Croatian on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that a copy of the instructions to municipal leaders dated December 19, 1991, that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you then tell Your Honours whether this document -- the significance of this document and whether it represented anything in terms of the municipal strategy you've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this document in comparison to the trajectory that the leadership was on on the -- at the session on the 11th of December, this -- these instructions move the principal organising body from the Bosnian Serb Assembly to the SDS itself, and thereby go from a legislative decision-making body into a party organ, where they were considered -- I wouldn't call it in secret, but in private. And they were also disseminated in private. So there is a move here from the legislative body to the party organ and from a very public discussion to the -- let's say circles -- inner circles of the party. In addition, it moves from expecting local leaders to form one institution, that is, the Bosnian Serb Municipal Assembly -- or the Serb Municipal Assembly to two institutions, one still being that Bosnian Serb -- or the Serb Municipal Assembly and the other being a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people, so from one institution to two. In addition, it tasked local SDS leaders to assume military functions in the terms of the instructions and it added considerable specificity to the steps to be taken by those municipal officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your Sarajevo report we've seen this document referred to as the Variant A and B document. Could you explain the significance of that description.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document distinguished between municipalities in which Serbs were in a majority and those in which they were not in a majority, thus the name A and B. And furthermore was to proceed in two stages. One was a preparatory stage and the other second stage was an actual implementation stage, which according to the terms of the document was to be activated by a secret signal from the party president.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you -- I note this document bears the number in the top right-hand corner 93, whereas in your Sarajevo report you cite to copy of this same document numbered 96. Is there any significance to the numbering of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the numbers apparently refer to the municipality to which the particular copy was distributed. I referred to number 96 in my paper. One in fact has a choice. I think there are something like seven copies all together that have been acquired from various municipalities. That copy 96 was found in the municipality of Trnovo, one of the Sarajevo -- one of the ten Sarajevo municipalities. This is number 93. It was found in the Holiday Inn offices of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this document acted upon by municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reaction to the distribution of this document was quite varied by municipality. There was also a convening of a committee for all ten municipalities of the city of Sarajevo in the days after the document was distributed. In some municipalities SDS leaders convened meetings within the next week and acted to pass along these instructions to various party members and move forward with the preparatory phase. Other municipalities, SDS leaders, did nothing; they just sat on their hands for some weeks and in some cases a couple of months. And in a few municipalities, there was outright resistance to implementing the instructions. I have described in my Sarajevo paper the particular situation in Centar municipality in Sarajevo, where the president of that municipality, Radomir Bulatovic, publicly refused to implement the instructions until he was basically found one -- found these institutions had been created without his direct participation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, one just quick follow-up question related to that. Do you know what happened to or did anything happen to Bulatovic as a consequence of that refusal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He suddenly found the formation of these institutions -- or at least of the Bosnian -- or the Serb Assembly to be a great idea and publicly endorsed it, reversing his earlier stand on this. And I don't believe there were any adverse consequences for him in the subsequent weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if you could kindly direct us to where in his Sarajevo report this document is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Footnotes 48 to 51 of his Sarajevo report, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before we move on, perhaps I could request that this be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, did any stage at the implementation of these instructions become mandatory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the -- at the 12th Assembly Session in March of 1992, the party leaders required that all municipalities -- actually, required that the regional organisations enforce the creation of these institutions in the various municipalities, and a resolution was passed to that effect by that Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard, perhaps I could ask that 65 ter number 00021, which is the transcript of the 12th Assembly Session dated 24 March 1992, be displayed. English page -- pages 22 to 24, so beginning with page 22; and B/C/S pages 39 to 42. And while we wait for that, can I just ask, Dr. Donia, when you referred to party leaders just now, who in particular did you mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Donia, do you see the excerpts from the 12th Assembly Session on the page in front of you in English and Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have reviewed this before and seen the entire document. And this is indeed a record of the 12th Session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to the fourth full paragraph, the large paragraph in the centre of the page, third sentence which begins: "We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I suggest we look at the speaker here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go back two pages I think. One page. My apologies. Wonderful. Do you see the speaker designated at the bottom of the page displayed in front of you, Dr. Donia, that's English page 21, Dr. Karadzic appears at the bottom of the page as the speaker?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now go back to the highlighted passage that I've just referred to on page 22. Thank you. Dr. Donia, this passage that begins: "We have a legal basis on the Law on Internal Affairs, and we also have the insignia and at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days." Is this one of the directions by the party leaders you've just referred to as regards the implementation of these instructions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This and the rest of this paragraph constitute one of the requirements that I have cited, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we now go over to English page 24, please -- I think it might be actually e-court page 23. I note at the bottom of e-court page 23 the speaker at this moment is the chairperson, which is who, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session it was Dr. -- or Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then over to the next page, 24, please. Perfect. Could I direct your attention, Dr. Donia, to the notation about just over one-third of the way down the page immediately after the sentence that is underlined which reads: "The chairperson explained that all the presidents of autonomous district had received instructions and should have prepared and organised this. Those who have not done it should do it by Friday." Is this one of the or the other direction by the party leaders you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Some time ago I went back to a calendar and it was a three-day period until Friday from the day of the Assembly. I'd also just like to clarify that I think I used the pleural in speaking of the institutions. This in fact -- this directive pertains to the formation of Serbian Municipal Assemblies and not to Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that this 12th Assembly Session be admitted, please, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat. I didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Chamber has already had the practice of admitting the transcript as a whole, the whole session, that it's all admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P961.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, these instructions that we've been discussing, could you tell us whether they were specifically discussed at subsequent Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions later in the war at sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, a few different speakers referred to the A/B instructions, and specifically Dr. Karadzic did on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask now for 65 ter number 00055, the transcript from the 50th Assembly Session of the -- 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly from 15 and 16 April, 1995. My notation says that the passage -- the relevant passage should be at pages 316 of the English and 278 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First page says the 34th Session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You know, Your Honours, I'm quite happy to come back to this and move on in the meanwhile. We can address this session after the break, and I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Shall we do that, Dr. Donia. I'll move on to another area and come back to this one exhibit later on today. I'd like to move on -- I'd like to ask you the next -- this next question. When do you recall first expressions of the intent to use violence by the Bosnian Serb leadership against Sarajevo or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that I could identify that point in time. There was a great deal of discussion of violence going back even to the period of the election campaign. There were a few references to it. I think in terms of, say, discussions of consistent and massive violence I would say there were a number of expressions of that in telephone conversations among SDS leaders in early September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was the context of those conversations, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From about the 2nd until the 9th of September, there were four crises in quite rapid succession in the boundary areas of Bosnia that drew the attention of SDS leaders. I think the one that's -- that was the most acute and the one that occasioned some of these statements was the detention of Mr. Milan Martic, who was the minister of the interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in Croatia. He was crossing a bridge and was detained by a patrol, taken to a police station in a tiny village called Otoka, and the police station was then surrounded by a crowd of principally Muslim local residents. It was a situation that was quickly escalating into a dangerous one, and in the subsequent hours, Dr. Karadzic tried to mobilise the Yugoslav national army, basically come in and rescue him, and also called upon Milan Babic, who was the head of the RSK at that time, to mobilise forces to be prepared to move into Bosnia to rescue him as well. That episode ended when a senior police official from Sarajevo, Avdo Hebib, arrived and police under his command essentially created a cordon, took him out of the jail, and escorted him out of town, that is, Mr. Martic out of town, and arranged for him to be transported to a Yugoslav People's Army installation nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, excuse me. Doctor, just to be clear, by telephone conversation, do you mean -- did you mean intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was this evidence of yours based upon the -- based upon those intercepts? Was your knowledge that you got from these -- hearing these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part, Your Honour. The periodical press covered this rather major event very closely. There were reporters from Glas newspaper in Banja Luka, "Oslobodjenje," and other publications that subsequently then gave very specific accounts of these events. And so the -- my summary of it that I just provided was based on a consolidation of those sources and the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually perhaps if I may, to follow-on with what you had -- from the question you've just raised, Your Honour. I remember yesterday, Dr. Donia, you identified four criteria for your selection of sources for your reports. And I wonder if it might be useful if you could explain how these and the other intercepts you've referred to in your reports might fit within those criteria.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- from my point of view, looking at the veracity of them, I was primarily interested in cross-checking the information referenced in the intercepts with other events going on as reported in the periodical press or other documentary sources. This particular incident, the cross-checkability is extraordinary and provides confirmation of a single story with very few details differing, not only between the periodical press accounts and the intercepts, but also among the various reports in newspapers of somewhat different political orientation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like now, if I may, to play an intercept from this period of time, 65 ter 30214 dated 9 September 1991, and I hope that my colleagues in the booth have been given copies of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it appears perhaps not because I don't hear the interpretation. Perhaps Mr. Reid can assist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It might be a technical problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or if it's convenient, we may take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We could do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope technical problems have been solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll try, Your Honours, but in the event they haven't we do have a backup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's try then, if we may, to play for you, Dr. Donia, an intercept of a telephone conversation from September 9, 1991, between Dr. Karadzic and Malko Koroman. Now, before we begin, could I ask you this: Do you know who Malko Koroman was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Koroman was at this time the head of the police in the municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we try that intercept now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Malko KOROMAN: Good afternoon. "Radovan KARADZIC: Good afternoon. "Malko KOROMAN: Malko Koroman from Pale speaking. How are you, Mr. Karadzic? "Radovan KARADZIC: Fine, thanks. How are you? "Malko KOROMAN: I apologise for calling you at this number. I have never done it so far but the situation has forced me to do so. "Radovan KARADZIC: Tell me. "Malko KOROMAN: Well, I heard this morning that Matic was blocked up there in Otoka. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Malko KOROMAN: Well, I would like to know what was done regarding that matter. I spoke to Banja Luka just now. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Malko KOROMAN: With this head of centre up there. "Radovan KARADZIC: Zupljanin? Zupljanin, right? "Malko KOROMAN: Ah, yes, Zupljanin. "Radovan KARADZIC: Right. "Malko KOROMAN: And he says that he's been blocked by the people in Otoka. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: Exactly, but it cannot be with somebody's direction and -- "Radovan KARADZIC: Well, the SDA direction, that -- "Malko KOROMAN: Yes. "Radovan KARADZIC: And we have, all night been in touch with -- all night. "Malko KOROMAN: Did you speak to Cengic about this by any chance? "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. I did last night and he was supposed to fly there with Zepinic this morning. "Malko KOROMAN: Well, Zepinic did not go. "Radovan KARADZIC: He didn't go, right? "Malko KOROMAN: He did not. You know Zepinic, he would not. This morning, you know what was done by the ministry, only Avdo Hebib got into the car somehow around 8.00 to go up there by car, as if by car he could make it to finish it. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: And please, you are to this -- Cengic freely, that if Mr. Martic is not released he is going to have all of the Romanija region above Sarajevo tonight. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: This is our personal opinion. Yes. I spoke to the Romanija guys and our attitude is that we are not going to let them get away with this because it means tomorrow they can do it to you or anyone in this way. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Now we'll tell him that now, but they said that they were going and I was -- told me that this Zepinic was going to go. I will call him now. "Malko KOROMAN: Just to let you know, he did not move now -- "Radovan KARADZIC: I will now -- "Malko KOROMAN: -- a finger at all, as they would say. "Radovan KARADZIC: I will call now. Come on. I will call the General Staff to -- because last night, yes, I spoke to Slobo too. He spoke to Kadijevic. "Malko KOROMAN: Could I be in touch with you to know what is at hand so they will not raise the people if there is no need? "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: And we'll raise it completely. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. You have to have it prepared, to have the people prepared if they fuck around, but I will. I will finish it by now. "Malko KOROMAN: Huh, say that to Mr. Cengic freely. "Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. It's a deal. "Malko KOROMAN: He can finish it with one phone call only. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. We know he can. "Malko KOROMAN: The fact that Avdo Hebib drives around their car and agrees with them on the way what he will do and how long he will be there and what will be there and he will -- "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: -- do that is their problem. "Radovan KARADZIC: I know that. Now we are completely familiar with their -- their slyness. I will -- yes -- "Malko KOROMAN: That please, do not do that. "Radovan KARADZIC: I will now, yes. "Malko KOROMAN: So that you know that's the way it is. "Radovan KARADZIC: We'll be in touch. We'll have the people prepared and not only you but all of Krajina will -- we will send them all to fucking hell because of this. "Malko KOROMAN: Shall I call this number again or will you call me at -- "Radovan KARADZIC: You will call this number, dial occasionally. "Malko KOROMAN: Call this number. "Radovan KARADZIC: It's a deal. "Malko KOROMAN: Thank you. "Radovan KARADZIC: Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you have any comment on the audio of the intercepted conversation you've just heard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe according to the press reporting at the time, Mr. Hebib did in fact arrive by helicopter, did not drive. That -- it appears to me in the conversation that this was very early in the day and perhaps the two interlocutors in the intercept, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Koroman, did not yet have that information. The assumption that Dr. Karadzic made was that this gathering around the police station in Otoka had been instigated by the SDA. I don't know whether that was the case or not. It was in a sense a test of Mr. Izetbegovic's dual roles as president and as party -- as president of the SDA and president of the Presidency, and in this particular instance in dispatching a professional policeman rather than a political leader, he clearly opted to try to view this as a police rather than a party matter. And it was in fact resolved by the use of policemen in Bosanska Krupa to take Mr. Martic out of that small police station and escort him through the crowd with the assistance of tear gas and under a hail of stones. The idea which came in this conversation from Mr. Koroman, Mr. Koroman was to use the prospect of the Serb population of Romanija, the mountainous area around Sarajevo, essentially to threaten the other side, the Muslim side, with dramatic and physical action in the event that they didn't release him to the custody of -- or release him into safety immediately. That was, I think, the essential point of this conversation and the reason for Mr. Koroman's call was to convey that willingness to rally his people to take that step in the event that Dr. Karadzic so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the chronology of these September 1991 intercepts that you've referred to in your Sarajevo report at footnotes 187, 188, 189, where would you place this intercept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the report in front of me. I wonder if perhaps you could provide it to me so I can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can do that and I can refer to the citations for you. Footnote 187 is an intercept of a telephone Karadzic between Karadzic and Babic 9 September 1991. 188, an intercept between Karadzic and one Gojko Djogo 12 October 1991. 189, same intercept, same date.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this conversation is noted in footnote 179, so prior to the three intercepts that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, keeping in mind Your Honours' guidance in regards to intercepts, I will not be asking to tender this at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless the Defence is willing to admit that part. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have it marked for identification, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P962.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move on then to another area more specifically related to Sarajevo, Dr. Donia I would like to ask you this: Was the -- was the municipal strategy implemented in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In the -- what I've called in my report the western approaches, that is, the six western-most municipalities of Sarajevo, the municipal strategy in its two primary components, that is, the implementation of the A/B instructions and the redrawing of municipal boundaries was probably fulfilled more thoroughly than almost anywhere else in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how so? How was that done?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all by the creation of Serb Municipal Assemblies in several municipalities, the creation of Crisis Staffs, and a thorough redrawing of municipal boundaries in the western part of the city so that essentially the map as it had stood in -- at the end of 1991 by the end of March 19 -- I would say April 1991 -- or 1992 was essentially unrecognisable. It was quite different. The further implementation of the municipal strategy was seen in that a number of leading municipal SDS civilian leaders were given military functions and in fact military commands and emerged in the course of the early months of the war as significant military commanders with specific areas of responsibilities and units reporting to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move now to some examples of the implementation that you've just cited, and in that regard could we see 65 ter number 01447, a November 1994 article in the news magazine of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior on an interview with Malko Koroman. Thank you very much. Dr. Donia, in preparation for your testimony today, have you seen this document previously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go then to e-court page 2, just about halfway down the page, and in the B/C/S version e-court page 3, second full paragraph left-hand column. I would like to draw your attention in the English section to the second full paragraph after the bolded portion that reads: "Everybody in the former MUP knew about Pale. They knew that when we do not allow anyone to nose around there without us knowing about that. In September 1991 we 'moved' the Pale municipality borders to Lapisnica, that is Brus on Trebevic, so as to protect all the Serbian places and the population that was in our territory." Dr. Donia, is this one of the examples of the different matters of implementation that you referred to, a redrawing of municipal boundaries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this isn't specifically what I had in mind. This is the delineation of a boundary that was to be protected or guarded by the police forces of that municipality as opposed to what I was considering as the redrawing of municipal boundaries to be -- with the municipality to be governed by a Serb Municipal Assembly. It's a closely related delineation of boundaries, but it's not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is this Malko Koroman interviewed in this article to your knowledge the same Malko Koroman who was identified in the intercept we've just listened to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be admitted, please, Your Honours, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, it will be admitted as --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P963, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With regard to deconstructing or -- deconstructing municipalities, perhaps I could ask for us to look at 65 ter number 21361, an article entitled: "Serbs Bade Their Farewells to Sarajevo," from "Oslobodjenje" dated 25 December 1991. Dr. Donia, do -- have you had an occasion to look at the document that appears on the screen in front of you in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the -- an article from the Sarajevo newspaper "Oslobodjenje." It's coverage of the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you place the discussion that this document records, the decision to separate Ilijas municipality from the city of Sarajevo in context, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this article is dated only a few days after the dissemination of the A/B instructions and is in part a report -- a report on the implementation of those instructions with the added feature that the newly formed Ilijas board elected to leave the city of Sarajevo, that is, withdraw as being one of the ten municipalities of the city and instead join the autonomous region of Romanija, which was the Serb-created alternate -- alternative to the city of Sarajevo with that -- with the name of the mountain range that is near the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did any other Sarajevo municipality take similar steps prior to this one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Pale had taken the same step in very late April of 1991, so about eight months prior to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to 65 ter number 30595, which is a transcript of an intercept between one Prodanovic and Jovan Tintor, and this intercept was referred to in your Sarajevo report at footnote 53. And do you recognise the document on the screen then in front of you, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe it is in footnote 53 of the report, but I recognise the intercept that's appeared on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to review this in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we could go to e-court page 5 of the translation and B/C/S page 7, please. In e-court page 5, just above the very large paragraph, Tintor's interlocutor Prodanovic asks about his house in Donja Vogosca and he's advised: "It belongs to SAO Romanija. Everything from Vrelo Bosne to Visoko, brother, all of it will be connected and incorporated into Romanija. Of course new municipalities will be made, a new municipality is already being made, Rajlovac, which will include Zabrdje and the area all the way up to Vrelo Bosne and over here to the Serbian Vogosca." A couple of questions in regard to this intercept. First of all, are you familiar with Tintor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tintor was a key leader of the SDS in the Vogosca municipality and later on went to assume a -- I believe a position in the government of the Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you comment on the expanse of territory covered by Tintor in his response to his interlocutor and that, in particular, the new municipality which will include Zabrdje all the way up to Vrelo Bosne and over here to Serbian Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure this means nothing without the map in front of us, but just to put this in context: Vrelo Bosne is -- means the source of the Bosnian river. It is a park and recreational area in the Ilidza municipality, and on the map we were looking at yesterday would be at the extreme left side of that map. The territory that he is referring here to would extend to the north and east to include the -- a broad swath of territory going through Rajlovac, which is a settlement just to the north of Ilidza and became a separate municipality in 1992 and over to Vogosca, which is the town directly to the north of down-town Sarajevo and a -- one of the ten municipalities of the city. So he's speaking about the creation of a new municipality in the context here of a large territorial sort of unimpeded territorial sweep where he -- are used that Serbs are in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just getting the number of the map because it's going to assist us when we deal with this next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that this intercept be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark this for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have the audio recording for this just for the record?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, we do not. Could we move next to a further intercept between Dr. Karadzic and one Grkovic dated 22 February 1992. That's 65 ter 30611. 30611, an intercept for which in fact we do have an audio file, but I'll not be playing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see the original B/C/S transcript of that intercept on the screen in front of you, and now the English one appears as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review those in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the intercept we just discussed in which Tintor was involved talked about the formation of the municipality of Rajlovac, and this intercept about two-thirds of the way down the first page - if we could scroll down, please, and it's also at the same location in B/C/S, thank you - Ljubo Grkovic tells his interlocutor, Dr. Karadzic, that he's just arrived from Reljevo saying: "We established a municipality down there ..." and further explains: "It will be called Rajlovac Serb municipality and includes R eljevo and everything until Vogosca and Ilijas and over here until Osijek and the television." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I want to refer you to the map you've just referred to, the map from yesterday, Dr. Donia, P815. P815, please. Because, Dr. Donia, perhaps you could comment on the expanse of territory covered by these two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both intercepts go to the creation of the Rajlovac municipality, which was carved out as a separate municipality from the existing municipality of Novi Grad. And that is of course in the -- just to the left centre, slightly above the centre of this map. And one sees here that the Novi Grad municipality encompassed considerable piece of territory in the western part of the city and went -- actually, existed both to the north and south of the main thoroughfares. The -- Rajlovac took its name from a settlement -- do I get to draw again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would invite you, if we could move past the experiences of yesterday with the map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Here. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Making a blue circle just to the left of the printed words "Novi Grad."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Rajlovac was in fact at one time in the early years of socialism a municipality on its own, but it was also this community which included an airstrip and an academy for air force instruction that was run by the Yugoslav People's Army. The new municipality of -- newly created municipality of Rajlovac also included Zabrdje, which was the family home of Mr. Krajisnik. And that is a little bit further north of the circle that I've just indicated along -- just inside the main road, roughly there. That's an approximation. So Rajlovac emerged as this new municipality on the Serb-drawn map of the western approaches as a large central area with considerable settlements but also a large swath of mountainous or very hilly territory where the words "Novi Grad" are on this map and to the north and east of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, if you could kindly put a letter R and Z respectively for future identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see. R and Zabrdje. Okay. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- thank you for that, Dr. Donia. And I wonder, although it might be difficult at this magnification, I wonder if you're in a position to indicate approximately on this map the television station so that Their Honours can get an idea of the breadth, the approximate breadth of the territory to encompass this new municipality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see here. I'm going to pick about here for the television station. I guess it's actually a little bit closer to the road rather than the railroad here, but that's approximately where it is. And the television -- what's called a television station is in fact a huge concrete structure that was pretty much despised for its architecture by everybody in Sarajevo and was nonetheless a very pronounced feature in the western approaches area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So from this succession of documents relating to Ilijas, Vogosca, Rajlovac area, what do you see as being a new configuration of the municipal boundaries of the western approaches to the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the new municipal boundaries as they ended up in early April of 1992 caused the municipalities to flank this main transportation or artery east-west rather than to flow across it, as was the case in the prior municipal organisation. So that was accomplished by eliminating Novi Grad, creating Rajlovac as a municipality wholly on the north side of the road, and taking part of Novi Grad that was south of the road and dividing it -- if I may just do this kind of conceptually. I really don't know exactly where the boundary ran, but taking part of it and including it in Novo Sarajevo and part of it -- and including it in Ilidza. This piece here actually -- the Dobrinja settlement was included in the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I could ask you, just as you've done with R, Z, and T for the television station, T and an arrow in fact, to mark Dobrinja with a D, perhaps Novo Sarajevo with NO, and Ilidza with an I? Would that be appropriate, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ilidza is I think already on the map and it was a matter of redrawing the boundary of Ilidza. Actually, that happened in mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in terms of this redrawing of municipal boundaries, do you see this as -- add rationale to the linkage or behind the linkage of these particular areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it removed municipal organisation from the business of having to transect -- or cross major thoroughfares and created municipalities which had both a, say, a demographic population base of -- that were substantial -- included substantial numbers of Serbs, and left some Muslim settlements which were -- there were really two of them that were largely Muslim, Sokolovic, Kolonija, and Sokolija [phoen] as enclaves within these newly designed municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this a peaceful process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the redrawing of the boundaries was not a violent act. It simply established new jurisdictions that challenged the governmental jurisdiction of the city of Sarajevo and of the existing municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You eluded earlier in your testimony to civilian leaders being given military functions in regard to the implementation of the municipal strategy. What was their role? What did they do in carrying out these functions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, they became commanders of units and led people from their municipalities in establishing the Siege of Sarajevo and in linking up the lines of the siege with other municipalities and defining the territories which were to come under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this a peaceful process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we move further, Your Honours, if I could go back to the intercept of 65 ter 30611 between Dr. Karadzic and Ljubo Grkovic of 22 February, 1992, I wonder if I could ask that be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So would you like to save this marking, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was just going to do that next, but as long as we catch both items, please. And I would like this map as marked by Dr. Donia to become the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P966.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be MFI P967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I may, on the subject of these civilian leaders who became commanders of units and led the people from their municipalities in establishing the siege lines, I'd like actually to play a video-clip now from 65 ter 45111 depicting an interview by Risto Djogo of Jovan Tintor dating from 1994. And before we begin the video, perhaps I could ask you this, Dr. Djogo -- Dr. Donia, are you familiar with Risto Djogo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a journalist who did a lot of interviews for I believe the Serbian television station in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could play this video, which will be the last video of this presentation today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Risto DJOGO: You were in control of Zuc at the time and everything else, Pofalici. How did you see the tragedy of the Serbian people in Pofalici? You were close by. "Jovan TINTOR: Well, you see, then war already began. I don't have two minutes of military education and kind of -- but I put myself at the head of this people as the commander and kind of civilian leader. I took the gun and organised the people the best I could. The front line I held was big. It wasn't only Vogosca. I believed that I should help all Serbs living on the territories where they weren't properly connected, so I held 64 kilometres of front line. From the Jezero hospital, that is, the child -- the maternity hospital through Vogosca over the middle, coming down on the territory -- a part of the territory of Ilijas, then back across Rajlovac, Ahatovici, and a part of Ilidza. The barracks in Butim were the first barracks that were left empty, so I took my units from Vogosca and filled the barracks so that it wouldn't stay empty, so they would not take that territory of ours. Because those were Serbs living there. So coming back over Sokolje again, Zuc, from Zuc, Vogosca, to Potonje, again all the way to Kobilja Glava. It's a huge territory. And I came to Zuc because I considered it to be a very important strategic point. With me and lucky for me or for us I had Colonel Vukota Vukovic with us who was the only officer of the JNA at the time, that is, one of the individuals who offered -- who put himself at the disposition of the Serbian Democratic Party, that is to say, the insurgents of Serbian Vogosca. He helped me at the very beginning, I mean the beginning of the organisation of people and organisation of the defence. We went to Zuc and we conquered that very important strategic point. And we connected up with Pofalici. However, once I officially asked from Pofalici representatives to come for a discussion, they came a few times, and one time I said that they had to -- they did not accept that plan. After that I issued the order twice, that they have to retreat, so that we can make an action and go down to the city. Because I was informed -- I was present at a meeting in Vrace where Mr. Kukanjac was supposed to be present too. I wasn't lucky enough to meet him at the time, but I met our present General Subotic, President Karadzic, President Krajisnik, Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic, and at that meeting we spoke about getting together to cut the city in two and, well, to enter the city using that bridge, the former Brotherhood and Unity Bridge."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Donia, before I ask you for comment on this clip, could you tell us if you're familiar with some of the names identified by Mr. Tintor. First, Mr. Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kukanjac was the JNA commander of the military district centred in Sarajevo which covered essentially all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also had some residual responsibility for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic was a member of the government of the Bosnian Serb republic when it was first proclaimed, and subsequently in I think April -- March or April became the minister of the interior of that government, essentially the top policeman in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the -- Mr. Mandic was the deputy minister of the -- of the Ministry of the Interior who later founded the separate Serbian Ministry of the Interior and police in late March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And finally, General Subotic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Subotic was a commander in the JNA who subsequently had a major command in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you have comment on this video-clip that we've just seen with regard to the theme we've been discussing of civilian leaders being given military functions or taking on military functions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he -- Mr. Tintor pretty well spelled out what those military functions included. They included establishing a line of defence, taking the strategic hill of Zuc in the very heart of the Rajlovac municipality, and linking up with other military units and leaders as a part of the plan to establish the ring around the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've explained earlier that Mr. Tintor held a function in Vogosca. Did situation that he's described and the tasks he's taken on, was that the case in other Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was similar process took place in Ilidza, in Ilijas, and in the general area of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could turn to a transcript of an intercepted conversation dated 21 May 1992, 65 ter 30788, between one Nedjeljko Prstojevic and Milisav Gagovic, and while we're waiting for that to come up, can I ask you, Dr. Donia, are you familiar with Mr. Prstojevic, do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic was the president, I believe, of the SDS party in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the intercept on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to review this intercept prior to -- in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to comment on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not seeing it all here, so I don't know exactly what -- without seeing the whole thing, I'm not going to be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move over to the next page, please. And scroll down. And I note, Dr. Donia, at the bottom of this page Mr. Prstojevic's interlocutor Gagovic notes that: "The Muslims are fleeing Dobrinja for no reason." And then if we could scroll over to the third page. At the top of the page I note Mr. Gagovic stating: "Yes, I ordered the press centre to release the information that we are allowing Muslims to leave Dobrinja, but as long as it's only entire families that are leaving. " And further down six cells up from the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Six cells up from the bottom Prstojevic says the words: "Check-point in Nedzarici," word missing, "through towards Bascarsija, they say there's a lot of living space there." Does -- do you recall now the context of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a conversation about the rather fast-moving events in the area of the western approaches, and indicates that the Muslim population from Dobrinja, which is this large housing complex, high-rise housing complex that was built for the 1984 Olympics, is proceeding with the approval and sponsorship, if you will, of the SDS leaders. The conversation then goes to talk about the check-point in Nedzarici, which is another location in the western approaches area, and the fact that there is a lot of empty space, presumably empty apartments in that area on the way toward -- toward the centre city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Dr. Donia, I could direct you to footnote 273 of your Sarajevo report, where I believe this intercept was cited.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. What -- I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add to your comments about this intercept, looking at the citation from your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the report I link this conversation with an event that was taking place at that time and the -- started I believe the 20th of May, in which a large convoy of a couple hundred -- or a few kilometres long sponsored by the children's ambassador in Sarajevo was detained as it left the city and retained -- or detained for two days while negotiations proceeded involving the Red Cross to allow the children and few women who were part of the convoy to exit the city. That convoy eventually was released I think on the 22nd or the 23rd of May, and it was -- it then proceeded I think to the Adriatic coast and left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I omitted to ask to tender the video which we played, 65 ter number 45111, timer number 00:22:05 to 00:26:22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit P968.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now not dealing with the tendering of that intercept for a moment, I'd like to turn to something Mr. Prstojevic said during the course of the 17th Bosnian Serb Assembly Session on 24 to 26 July 1992, and that is at D00092, page 66 in English and 66 in the B/C/S. Thank you. Dr. Donia, could I direct your attention in English and in B/C/S to the passage towards -- no, on the bottom half of the page, please, where you see Prstojevic and a colon on both sides - thank you - where halfway down the paragraph in which Mr. Prstojevic begins speaking, he notes: "Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learned that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a majority." And ask if you have any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in one sentence here Mr. Prstojevic has summarised a lot of what happened in the western approaches simultaneously with the establishment of the siege of the city and the conquest of most of the territory in the western approaches.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you find this statement to be reflective of any policy on the part of the SDS leaders around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a policy of ethnically cleansing the territories which they conquered and removing the non-Serb populations from most of those territories. It further indicates that the stated goal of previous months of acquiring only Serb land was in fact considerably exceeded in carrying out the action that he's describing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In that regard, perhaps I could ask that we - staying with the same session - go to e-court page 19 of the English and page 16 of the B/C/S. Now, if you could enlarge the bottom of the page, please, I have to count up the number of lines. I'm looking for the 19th line up from the bottom on this English page, and I see it. Dr. Donia, could I direct your attention to a statement by Dr. Karadzic here at the 17th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you could please, Mr. Registrar, display the left-hand side of the English page. It's a little difficult to see and it's cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
