utterances.text: And I think the 19th line up Dr. Karadzic says: "We do not have any more reason to fight. We have liberated almost everything that is ours. In final talks we could even return some territories, villages that do not belong to us." It's been very hard to identify that passage when we don't have any paragraph indentations, but are you familiar with that passage, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the Assembly session and as part of it familiar with this excerpt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment in relation to this statement by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he's stating here that the Bosnian Serb nationalist conquest of territory has gone considerably beyond what had previously been the territorial claims based on the identification of Serb lands. I think it also could be taken as an indication that Dr. Karadzic conceived of this additional land as bargaining chips for arriving at a territorial settlement to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we could move briefly to the very final area of questioning, I'd like to recall that yesterday in commenting on Dr. Karadzic's articulations of 12 May 1992 at page 3079, line 2 and onward, you said that Dr. Karadzic valued this separation of the city - referring to Sarajevo - as a way of crippling or denying -- crippling the state or denying to the Bosnian -- to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina the attributes of a state." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard could I ask that we look at 65 ter 11570. It's an interview with Stanislav Galic in Sarajevo Srpske Novine, dated 25 March 1994 entitled: "Aggression in Blue." And while we wait for that, I take it you know who Stanislav Galic is, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic was at that time the commander of the Romanija Corps which was besieging Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I -- do you see the interview on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that in preparing for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to page 6 of the translation in English, please, and just for the record page 2 of the B/C/S, the bullet point in the middle column. Now that we see the English translation in front of us, I'd like to direct you to the question of the interviewer that appears at the top of the page which says: "Many people say that the keys to war or peace are held in Sarajevo. What do you think about lifting the blockade of the city?" And the sixth line down from that General Galic responds: "As long as we have Sarajevo in such a territory, Alija has no state." Do you see that in the sixth line down from the interviewer's question?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on that statement and General Galic's articulations in this article as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular passage he is echoing a thing -- a statement that Dr. Karadzic frequently made about the -- his observation that most civil wars end up in some sort of negotiated settlement without a winner or a loser, and that Sarajevo is the critical point, critical area, for the ultimate resolution of the war. He then goes on to say that the critical issue in Sarajevo is to deny Izetbegovic a state and -- or polity with the attributes of a state and that therefore the Sarajevo -- Sarajevo will be central in any subsequent negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I tender this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P969.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one final question for you, Dr. Donia, have you seen evidence in these Assembly sessions and elsewhere that the strategic objectives that we began our presentation with guided Bosnian Serb army operations during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are numerous references to the importance of the strategic objectives in statements by military leaders, including most significantly General Mladic, before the Bosnian Serb Assembly and also in some of the -- I think the concepts of the strategic objectives are reflected in some of the general orders that guided the military offensives in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see, please, 65 ter 00085, the transcript from the 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, dated 15 and 16 April 1995, and I'm looking for page 22 of the English, please. Now, I -- and -- my apologies. It's B/C/S page 18. Dr. Donia, I'd like to direct your attention to this statement by General Mladic that's recorded on this page and the large full paragraph in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're going to have to scroll down, please, Mr. Registrar, and you're going to have to centre the English on the page, please, just a little bit better. No, it's going too far over to the left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the last sentence in this large paragraph which reads: "The tasks of the army in this war stem from the known six strategic objectives adopted by our Assembly which have not been carried out to the full due to the lack of material or other support"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this one of those statements by General Mladic regarding the strategic objectives that you've referred to and seen over the course of your research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move this session, please, the 50th, into evidence then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a whole? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P970.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And subject to any questions Your Honours may have, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you like to start now or do you like to have a break before you start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's all the same, then it would be better to take the break now and then to work until the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, have we admitted the report of the doctor, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my apologies, my sincere apologies. Your Honours, it would be appropriate for me at this moment to move -- to request to move the three reports, 65 ter number 11699, that's the origins of the Republika Srpska report; 65 ter number 11700, which is the -- what we've called the excerpts report throughout the presentation of this evidence; and 65 ter number 21894 into evidence. And at the same time, Your Honours will recall there is of course the matter of originally 19 - now I think 18 - exhibits which were identified in appendix B in our notification and exhibits list which we filed for Dr. Donia in February of this year. A number of those documents, Your Honour, I think three, I can perhaps stand to be corrected if I turn to my copy of the filing beside me, are transcripts of intercepted communications relating to the September incident Dr. Donia was discussing in his evidence earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By appendix B, do you refer to the several documents in the -- attached to Sarajevo report, including maps?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. By appendix B I'm referring to our filing of 5 February 2010, which attached two lists of documents, those which we would be referring to -- we would be using in evidence with Dr. Donia and a further 19, as I said now I think 18, selected sources used by Dr. Donia in compiling the reports for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me be clear. How many are there for items that would be using in evidence, 18 and further 19? So have you used all 18 or are you suggesting to tender those documents which were not used during the course of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Appendix A was the -- is the list of documents from which we drew the evidence we've exhibited during the course of Dr. Donia's presentation today; and appendix B is exactly as you've described, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear from the Defence. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, with respect to the second report of Dr. Donia, the excerpts, we note that in the Perisic case the Trial Chamber excluded that because it was not really an expert report. If you -- we believe that the underlying Assembly session records should be admitted, and if you find it convenient to have excerpts from Dr. Donia, then you certainly can admit the report if you would like. And we would seek probably when we have Defence expert witnesses to use the same procedure. So we don't have any particularly strong objection, but we do note in another instance it has been rejected. If I can -- also I wanted to turn to the appendix B, but perhaps Mr. Tieger can address this point now if he would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In that connection we have had the opportunity to discuss this matter with Mr. Robinson, and we certainly don't suggest that the excerpts report should come in without the benefit of the underlying Assembly sessions. And to provide the Court with a broader overview of this, pursuant to the Court's encouragement following the decision on further guide-lines for admission, we did meet with Mr. Robinson to discuss the possibility of reaching agreement on certain documents. I'm sure it won't surprise the Court, given what it's already heard about the Assembly sessions, that those were the first items on our agenda for agreement. And we agreed to, at least momentarily, defer the submission of a joint -- joint submission in connection with the Assembly sessions because of Dr. Donia's testimony and reports, concluding that it would be preferable to seek to jointly agree to the admission of those Assembly sessions referenced in Dr. Donia's reports. And I would note that all of the Assembly sessions, I'm advised by Mr. Sladojevic, appear on the list of Defence documents to be cross-examined, another reflection of the significance regarding those documents and the anticipation by the parties of their extensive use during the course of these proceedings. So again, to follow-up on Mr. Robinson's comments, we didn't anticipate that the excerpts report would come in without the benefit of the underlying Assembly sessions, and we agree that they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the remaining documents, other parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. With respect to appendix B, I note that at least one of those documents has already been admitted, directive 3, I believe, was admitted through cross-examination, so perhaps that list might have to be paired a little bit. But also I would note that it seems to fall outside of the guide-lines of the Chamber since it wasn't put to the witness, and he's not actually a 92 ter witness. But having said those things, once again we do encourage the admissibility of documents which seem to be relevant to the case and these do seem to be relevant. So if you're willing to see that something outside your guide-lines may nevertheless be admitted, we don't have any problem having the documents in appendix B admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no objection to the reports themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will give our ruling after the break. We will break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the -- given the reports are his product of his expertise and also the -- that basically there was no objection from the Defence and finally that particularly in relation to the thematic excerpts, although they are the collection of excerpts, the manner it is organised or categorised can be viewed as an exercise of his expertise. So we will admit the three reports, all of them. And as to the appendix B, we are satisfied with the probative value or reliability and that is the way it is tendered is consistent with our guide-lines and our previous decision. But certain items have been already admitted and the -- being consistent with our practice, we will not admit the intercepts, and I don't think we need to mark for it, given that they are not played during the court session. As for the appendix A, which was supposed to be used during the examination-in-chief, we will admit only those part that were actually used during the -- during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dobra dan."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that you speak our language, so it will be easier for us to understand each other. Tell me, please. What case is this for you, I mean in which you're testifying, number what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain exactly, but I think it's about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me how was it that you established contact with the OTP and the Tribunal? Did they seek you out or did you recommend yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1997 I received a phone call from a Prosecutor, asking if I was interested in considering testifying in the Blaskic case. So that was initiated by the Prosecution. I was employed in other things at the time and didn't have much interest in doing it at first, but indeed did pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you come to their minds? What was it that recommended you to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand from speaking with them further that I was recommended by Dr. Dennison Rusinow who is a long -- was a long -- he passed away a few years ago, a long-time scholar of the former Yugoslavia, lived for a long time in Zagreb and wrote a number of books and many individual articles about the history of the region. They spoke to him. He was, for I don't know what reasons, either not selected or chose not to participate and so he recommended me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time you were in Merrill Lynch in actual fact, but you were certainly not a scholar. You were not involved in history at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was it that guided this gentleman to recommend you? Could he not have thought of someone who was actively engaged in history at some institute?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rather suspect he did. He may have given them several names to suggest. I really don't know. We had known one another well for at that point 20 years, so he knew my -- not only my writings but my other activities in life and teachings. So I would assume that he was -- I was one of several people that he suggested to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So he was aware of your writings and of your views; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that at first you were not very keen on this. What was your motive to accept this after all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't keen on it because I had a full-time job and was otherwise engaged, but I did agree to just come and explore and see what the work entailed. I knew at that point that I wouldn't have time to pursue really much independent research or preparation, but could perhaps call on my knowledge at that point. So the question in my mind was whether I would be able to take the time to do the preparation that they would require for work that I'm doing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have to leave your old job then or did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stayed in that position until -- to say this was 1997 when I interviewed with them, I stayed in that position until the fall of 2000, my position with Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you leave them then or was it that Merrill Lynch faced difficulties then or was it that they faced difficulties later after all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to say that everything was fine when I was there. They in fact did face severe difficulties later on, but I probably left at about the best time prior to the down side to -- both in the market as a whole and at the firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what have you been doing since then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I teach occasionally. I've taught one course at the University of California at San Diego. I've taught on numerous occasions at the University of Michigan. I've done -- probably devoted the bulk of my time to research and writing in the ten years since I left Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can one make a living like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can make a living having worked for Merrill Lynch. One cannot make a living doing the things that I have been doing since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me who provided the titles to those works of yours, your studies and reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you the author of these works?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm not the author of the excerpts, but I'm the author of the two reports and selected the excerpts as indicated to in a sense make it a coherent narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not a scientific work, a scholarly work - correct me if I'm wrong - but it is a professional work based on scientific truths. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too sure what the difference is. I certainly followed the normal professional procedures in preparing all three reports and tried to adhere to the canons of the professional in preparing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you given an assignment by the Prosecution; and if so, how was the assignment worded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in each case in which I've been involved, I have first sat down with the Prosecutor and discussed what the Prosecutor wanted in terms of a report, by which I mean what the topic was to be, if there was a question of the chronological framework within which the report should be confined or a particular municipality or set of municipalities or the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. It just depended on what the Prosecutor requested. My feeling was that it is up to the Prosecutor to outline, essentially set the boundaries, of where my reports would lie. It's my job then to work within those boundaries to create an account as best I can from the sources and information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what are your obligations towards the OTP in general terms? Do you have to adhere to their views and the tasks that they set you and live up to their expectations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to prepare a report within the guide-lines that they establish, they set. Those guide-lines are not qualitative or they don't prescribe any particular viewpoint, but -- so I'm free to have different views or interpretations, both in the written reports and testimony, and actually have never been asked to adhere to a particular viewpoint, either in the report or my oral -- verbal testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could we get hold of those guide-lines perhaps, the guide-lines that they provided you with, the Prosecution I mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in -- I think in every case, they were verbal. They were a result of a discussion between us. And so there's no written guide-lines that have ever been provided to me that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We received some correspondence, so I was asking about the instructions and guide-lines. But anyway, who chose the material that you were to study?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of it I acquired myself. The exception being the documentation that's provided to me by the Prosecution typically at my request, which usually starts out with a very general request and gets more specific as I'm carving out the report itself. So my -- I think what I bring to the table perhaps more than anything else is a lot of use of independent sources, sources that the Prosecution may think are inconsequential or not available to them or in other ways are not a part of their database.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have an insight into all the material that you wanted to see? Did you decide on the selection of material or did somebody propose what they thought you should look at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'd say I've never been 100 per cent fully satisfied with what I was given. I have asked for a great deal and been given a great deal, but usually there was something else that I wish I had and sometimes something that occurs to me much later on that I wished I had asked for. But in general, I would say the Prosecution has responded to my specific requests for documentation on the themes that I'm working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that you devoted quite a lot of attention to statements made in newspapers and in interviews. Now, do you agree - and we should check this out first - whether the statements were authorised, whether they were accepted or disputed? And when someone gives statements to newspapers, they usually have a political note and are usually different to what we say when we're under oath. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a few different questions there. Do I check to see if the statements were authorised. You mean the statements that are published in the periodical press?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, did somebody actually say what the newspaper printed or was it the journalist's interpretation of what was said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the newspapers that I consulted, the journalist normally distinguishes between a direct quote or what specifically was said and the interpretation. Now, not every newspaper does that, I recognise, but I've mainly been using sources that follow that journalistic canon. And so I would -- for example, speeches that you've made, there are a lot of direct quotes, and I have relied on those quotes or press releases, things like that. But to be honest I didn't call you up and ask you if you had said those things. Your number was unlisted through much of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree with me that statements and speeches, that they have a political goal as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you have an insight into the documents and the behaviour of other parties in the conflict, just like those that you studied on the Serb side, analogous to those?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have and have paid some attention to them, but in the cases of the reports before us they weren't my primary target and area of interest. As you may know, I've prepared some reports about the HVO, Herceg-Bosna, essentially the Croatian nationalist undertaking. And for studying those, that movement, I used documents of that party. I'm familiar with many of the other sources for the study of other parties, including the social democratic party and the left opposition and the SDA. I have not consulted the vast majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you mentioned that it was the job of a historian to study the cause and effect, relationship, and to look at the context of issues - you mentioned that yesterday I believe. Did you do that in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that the Serbs - and then you quoted my words - saying that we waited for them to make a mistake or make a move and then we responded with a counter measure. Now, our counter measures, when you showed them did you show what caused these counter measures and caused that kind of conduct on our part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, yes; and in others no I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why not in all cases?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't central to the story or sufficiently central to fulfil the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I hope we'll arrive at that together now. But a personal question now. What are the earnings per case and per day in this job?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it relevant, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Your Excellency, that it is indeed and you'll see why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I think you need to tell us why before the witness answers the question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because we're all human beings, and if you imagine that Mr. Donia did something that the Prosecution didn't like, would he be testifying 15 times? Certainly not because they have their own interests in all of that. So I'm interested in knowing how come the Prosecution has some favourite witnesses and keeps bringing them back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't think it's relevant. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in your report about Sarajevo, Mr. Donia, on page 2 you speak about nations and nationalist movements. Do you distinguish between national and nationalistic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good question. It's a distinction that is a major one in B/C/S. And when I'm addressing these issues in B/C/S I usually use the term "national." And I'm very reluctant to call anything nationalist -- nationalistic. In English to me the distinction is somewhat different. In fact, there's very little distinction. So I freely use the term "nationalist" to describe all three parties, for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to distinguish them from what I conceive of as non-nationalist political formations and non-nationalist attitudes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the three parties that you talk about are not nationalist, but national, if we look at the Serbian language; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call them that, yes. I would use that term in describing them, and I do when I am using that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's not a disqualification of any kind, it's not a value judgement, political judgement, to say nationalist movement using the English?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my intent, that it not be judgemental. It's not a condemnation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next what I'm interested in is a paragraph where you opt for Professor Paula Pickering's position, and she considers that we're not born in a nation and that cultural identity does not exist, but that a nation -- a nation is an environmentalist creation or socially conditioned creation. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as you just quoted this excerpt, yes. I used that very brief passage to summarise what I consider a vast school of thinking about the constructed nature of nations or peoples and would kind of let her stand for this group of people that includes Benedict Anderson, Rogers Brubaker, Ron Sunia [phoen], and a host of other scholars who think of nations in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at one point - and we'll come to that - you said you were very happy when you saw that these ethnic borders aren't visible between municipalities or among municipalities. So I wanted to ask you: Is this your basis for opting for Ms. Pickering's view, is that your basis for the standpoint, too, to the effect that the Croats and Serbs in Bosnia should have agreed to create a new nation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as I understand your question to be that -- or you're asking me whether I opt to quote Professor Pickering because of my view that -- or it is my view that the Serbs and Croats wouldn't agree to form a new Bosnian nation, that would be wrong. I kind of start the other way around. Looking at the current thinking about nations and peoples, to approach and better understand the nature of nationalism and the three nationalisms in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree with Edouard Balladur, the former prime minister of France, and I do I believe that this is the position of other scholars, that a nation starts by superseding tribalism and tribes within one national group, that that is transcended?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a very partial statement of how nations develop, yes, I would agree with that but I would say it's very incomplete, particularly in the light of our current understandings of how nations are formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that nations were formed in the 19th century and that it is difficult to form a new nation in the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's always difficult to form a new nation, and the point is that nations are always in flux. They can appear and disappear and they are always changing their boundaries, their content, and for that matter the programmes of their political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us put aside the fact that you've probably heard of -- well, you know about Jung's work and Zondi's on the collective familiar subconscious and unconscious and Freud's views, that this is -- would you agree that this is just one-sided and that we should quote other authors that have -- that talk about other effects, apart from the social and the environmental in the creation of a nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're wading into an area about which there is a huge literature and many differences of opinion in terms of exactly how many and what elements should be included in examining the origins and development of a nation. You are citing people that you know better than I do in terms of their psychological expertise, and certainly it would be true that a comprehensive study of how a particular nation arises and develops should take into account the psychological viewpoint of those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you nonetheless think that the Serbs and Croats should have accepted an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina as a unitary state as conceived by the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should have accepted, well things would have been much simpler if they had. I don't know that the premises of your question -- that I would agree with all of them. I don't necessarily think that the conception of the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic is best described as a unitary state, but I would I guess point out that this is really the -- goes to the heart of the difference between what happened in the former Yugoslavia and what happened as the Soviet Union broke apart, where the independence of the various republics that made up the Soviet Union, which contained in them about 25 million Russians in the near abroad, did not contest the independence of the republics in withdrawing from the Soviet Union and didn't have the kinds of linkages with the leadership of the parent republic. That was the case in Yugoslavia. That it was a huge difference and many of those leaders of the Russian communities in the near abroad, in fact, participated in the push for independence. So it is not out of the question that one should think that the Serbs could have accepted an independent state and lived happily in it, but do I think they should have -- I wouldn't presume to prescribe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'm sure you agree that the Soviet Union was created in one way and Yugoslavia was created in a different way, with the Trianon Agreement, the Saint-Germain Agreement after the First World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were created in two different ways, and of course Yugoslavia was created twice and a different time each way -- or a different way each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that other way, was it a democratic way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the Serbs in Krajina and Bosnia would have accepted to remain in those republics if the condition for that had not been the existence of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not -- I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is the following: Croatia was formed from Croatia and the Serbian Krajina, and the Serbian Krajina was given to the Serb people by Austro-Hungary. And the Serbs agreed to become -- to join Croatia, but they were a constituent people. In all the post-war years, it was a dual-nation republic of the Serbs and the Croats. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's several questions here. The assumption that the Serbs were a constituent people is of course a statement out of Yugoslav constitutional theory, and I don't have any problem agreeing that under that theory they were a constituent people of Yugoslavia. The issue of whether they were a constituent people in Croatia, I'm just afraid I'm not able to answer because I don't pretend to be an expert on the constitutional theory of the -- of either Croatia or the former Yugoslavia. I wouldn't agree with your formulation about the Serbian Krajina being given to the Serb people by Austro-Hungary. That's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Serbs were given autonomous rights in Austro-Hungary for having defended the area from the Turks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't given autonomous rights by Austro-Hungary because Austro-Hungary didn't exist before 1867. The Krajina area was, in fact, the beneficiary of autonomous rights, which drew many Serbs to the area to populate the military frontier region. And they were engaged in military actions at times, usually with people on the other side who in many cases were Serbs as well. So I wouldn't agree with the formulation that they were actually fighting against the Turks as their -- certainly not as their sole activity in manning the military frontier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that we can agree that it was Austria first and then Austro-Hungary later. But we're not disputing the fact that the Serbs were given autonomous rights in Krajina, today's Krajina, and that they were given them by Austria; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to get the chronology right, the -- most of those -- many of those Serbs actually relocated, migrated, or moved to the area and were rewarded with the autonomous rights particularly of the church, the Serbian Orthodox church, and some administrative autonomy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the interpretation. That's why I paused for a moment. But do you know who the "ktitor" of the Krka monastery, the head priest of the Krka monastery? It's the Orthodox monastery.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The endowment. That was far before Austria, the Nemanjic dynasty and endowment. But let me ask you this, Mr. Donia: Do you know how those lands became united, the lands which were within Austro-Hungary? Vojvodina was different, but today's territory of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, how they united with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the actual proclamation of Yugoslavia which was on 1 December 1918 brought those lands together with the Kingdom of Serbia and Montenegro to form the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But how did they unite? Do you agree that before that a state was formed of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in this united area, this united territory, and that that territory united with Serbia. It didn't last long, but it has to be established so that America would agree to the united state ultimately.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a number of questions there. I think I just described how the state was actually formed. It was formed by proclamation of the Serbian prince regent Aleksandar on December 1, 1918. It -- there certainly were -- there was a Yugoslav committee formed prior to the proclamation in the course of the First World War, and the Corfu declaration of 1917 set the stage in a sense for that unification, but the act itself was a -- not really a -- didn't have a whole lot to do with the international, let alone, American participation in creating the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us try to clarify this. Do you agree that the Nis declaration and the Korfu declaration in actual fact meant that the Serbs had given up on creating Serbia, rather they advocated the creation of a joint state of the southern Slavs? That's a pretty easy question. It can be answered just by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how were things then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think many Serbs saw the Yugoslav state as an expanded Serbia and saw no inconsistency between wanting to see an expanded Serb state and calling it the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. So I wouldn't -- I can't agree with you that the Serbs gave up on creating Serbia at that point. That would not be consistent with the flow of events that resulted in the creation of the kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us then, after 1918 when did Serbia first come into being, the Banovinas included. Serbia disappeared in 1918, it melded into Yugoslavia, but when did it reappear?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question. I guess it first reappeared as a separate polity in 1941, and as the -- through the creation of the German occupation. There were certainly -- one of the Banovinas favoured Serbia to be sure, but that really was not a separate polity. And then after that would have come into -- came into being with the proclamation of socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree that that Serbia, Nedic's Serbia, came into being on the basis of the remnants that were left over after the dismembering by the neighbours carried out, that this is what was left over after all the neighbours of Serbia dismembered Serbia and this was what was left over and then Nedic was compelled to become prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how was it then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- you know, the -- the Serbian occupation polity under Nedic was a -- was indeed a creature of convenience for the German occupiers, but I wouldn't describe it as all that was left after the neighbours had dismembered Serbia, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Hungary take Vojvodina then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Bulgaria take Macedonia and parts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bulgaria did take effectively all of Macedonia and a little bit of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Albania take Kosovo as assisted by Italy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of it, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia take Zemun and did it get to the other side of the river viewed from Belgrade, all the way to Zemun, all the way to Zemun? Zemun and Zagreb were territorially linked. It was contiguous territory in a single country?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Serbia was dismembered, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbia didn't exist before that. Yugoslavia was partitioned by the occupying powers, and parts of it were given to neighbouring states that were considered allies or allies of the Germans and Italians in 1941. So I don't know that you can talk about Serbia being partitioned when it as a polity didn't exist at that time. It was a dismemberment of Yugoslavia that took place, and each part that was sort of hived off was given to someone else or stood alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia take all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and part of Srem and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably put it that all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and part of Srem were given by the German occupiers and to some degree the Italian occupiers to the independent state of Croatia. I don't know that Croatia was in a position to take anything at that point other than what they were given to administer by the Germans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the independent state of Croatia, the NDH, that's a very important subject. But now let me ask you this: Do you remember what it was that the Allies offered to Yugoslavia in the London Agreement of 1915 -- actually, what it was that they offered to the Serbs? Yes, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that their offer to the Serbs was a western boundary of the Serb lands along the Virovitica-Karlobag-Karlovac line?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection or knowledge of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is a very important point because Serbia had suffered a great deal and the western Allies had made an offer to Serbia to forget about Slovenia and Croatia and to create a Serbia, and in Corfu they made a different decision, they passed the Corfu Declaration. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I can't confirm that or don't have the information to either agree or disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Those are historical facts. We'll deal with that easily. You mentioned the Yugoslav committee. Do you know that the Yugoslav committee existed in Zagreb and in Split -- actually, do you know about that, that they existed in Zagreb and in Split and the one in Zagreb consisted of Slovenes as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav committee had representatives I think from Slovenes, Croats, I think even one Bosnian or two -- maybe one or two Bosnian members, and Serbs. It was a committee made up of people who were preparing to come together to form the kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Split committee had blackmailed the Zagreb committee? They said either go and strike a deal with the Karadjordjevics or we will decide to the effect that Dalmatia will join Serbia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D1369 or 1? What was it? 1361.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you remember the 14 points of Woodrow Wilson, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't name them, no. I know there were 14 and that he was famous for them, so to that degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Serbian version as well -- oh, no, there isn't one. Sorry. So then can we just have one so we can see it better in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can agree -- or rather, you will agree that on the 8th of January, 1918, President Woodrow Wilson presented his 14 points to the US Congress and that they contained a basis for achieving a lasting peace in Europe; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his intent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what he made public and that was what paved the way for the end of the First World War. The US was always a major power, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It certainly -- the United States played an important role in the latter, particularly in the latter year and a half or two of the First World War and was an important player in the diplomatic arrangements that were brought about, but not as -- let's -- let me just say the principles that you see here that Wilson laid out were probably not as influential as some idealistic historians have proposed in actually ending the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you do accept that there are such historians who claim that these 14 points were the basis for the establishment of peace in Europe and for Germany's surrender; right? It's a large number of historians who believe that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No so many anymore, but certainly there have been.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a bit. Can we -- yes, yes. We need that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Donia, that the principle of self-determination of nations was established then and it was proposed by America through its very president, Woodrow Wilson?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree it was established then. I would concur that it was proposed by Woodrow Wilson in this document and that it seriously failed in the actual application of the principles to the making of the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this principle of the self-determination of peoples and nations part and parcel of the international covenant on human rights? Did anyone else propose that before Wilson? Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it was around before Wilson. The principle, of course, of self-determination of peoples is -- goes back much further than this, but the -- it's also, you know, one of several principles which often enter into conflict in the -- both the sense of international law, but also more importantly - and I wouldn't speak to the international law side of it - but in the actual implementation of agreements based on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the principle of self-determination of peoples is part of the international covenant on human rights?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to read point 11 out of the 14.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rumania, Serbia, and Montenegro should be evacuated; occupied territories restored; Serbia accorded the free and secure access to the sea; and the relations of the several Balkan states to one another determined by friendly counsel along historically established lines of allegiance and nationality; and international guarantees of the political and economic independence and territorial integrity of the several Balkan states should be entered into."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Donia, that your country owes us access to the sea?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you see, we want the right to access to the sea and we carried it through, through the establishment of two Yugoslavias, but now we, that is to say, Serbia and Republika Srpska, are landlocked.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're suggesting that on the basis of Woodrow Wilson's proclamation of 1918 that the United States owes any country in 2010 access to the sea, I think that's kind of an absurd proposition. The nature of this document is not a promise for all time and eternity; it's a set of guide-lines that Wilson hoped would lead to a conclusion of the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only Wilson. It was accepted by both the House and the Senate; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much good to say about either of those right now either, but that still would not make it a policy commitment of the United States for all time and eternity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you what was promised in 1915 to the Kingdom of Serbia by the London Conference -- or rather, the Allies, Britain, France, and Russia, before the revolution broke out. The Dalmatian coast from Krka to Ston was promised to the Kingdom of Serbia. Do you know that that coast had belonged to the Serbian Emperor Dusan; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked two questions, one about the London Agreement or London Conference of 1915, and I indicated that I'm not aware of what the London Conference promised or if it promised anything at that time. Was the Dalmatian coast from Krka to Ston belonged to the Serbian Emperor Dusan, I think much of it did. Frankly, that was a time when maps didn't have a whole lot of meaning in that regard, and it's been owned and occupied by a number of different polities both before and since then. So I wouldn't want on that basis to conclude that it should be part of Serbia today or at any time after that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that occupation is one thing and an integral part of a state with a population that speaks the same language and that share the same religion is a completely different matter. So it is from that point of view that that area belonged to the Serbia of Emperor Dusan at the time and that is quite different from foreign occupation; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with your characterisation of the Serbian empire under Dusan as a state with a population that all spoke the same language and shared the same religion. I think that's a stretch, a real stretch, to suggest that. And I didn't refer to foreign populations. I said that the area has been owned and occupied by a number of different polities, both before and since then and Venice among them. But -- the Ottoman Empire in parts. The fact that a given piece of real estate was at one time part of any polity doesn't mean that it should -- that that polity should reacquire that territory six centuries later. That's just a -- I think a kind of a contentious use of the historical record to suggest a territorial claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you should tell the Allies that. You should have said it to them in London in 1915. Emperor Dusan stated which the languages of his empire were. He bore the title of the king of Serbs and Arbanians and Greeks; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably was not in a position to say much to the London Conference in 1915. I don't know what Emperor Dusan's title or position really has to do with the issue of territorial claim. The fact of the matter is that kings acquired titles periodically throughout their reign, lost them again, and so I think on the basis of a king holding a title to a piece of territory six centuries ago doesn't really represent a very convincing claim to territory today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, albeit very interesting, we've been into this historical discussion for more than an hour. When will we come to 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're getting there, Excellency. I just want to put the following to Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are not saying all of this for the sake of Emperor Dusan; rather, that was the basis for making an offer to Serbia in 1915 and it consisted of the following, the Dalmatian coast, and you know that there was a large Serb population there, Split, Brac, all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srem, Backa, Slavonia -- well, Slavonia although Italy opposed it, and some parts of Albania. So in 1915 Serbia refused that. That is the information that they received on the 4th of August, 1915, but Serbia refused that all for the sake of the pan-Yugoslav idea. Isn't that the case, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. But I don't know who I'm going to discuss this with if you don't know about this. Now, let me remind you of something else. The state of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, was it not proclaimed with the intent of unifying with Serbia if it was proclaimed as a united state. The Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, did they not constitute this state that came into being? These were territories that were set free with the decline of Austro-Hungary, along with the 14 points of Woodrow Wilson.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this state consisting of three peoples, did it include Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes -- or rather, the other way around, Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs? Were they equal? Were they constituent peoples? Did they constitute that state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's three questions that I hear. It was in fact Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was the name of the kingdom, not the other way around. The nationality policy of the state was that these were three tribes of one people, Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes being those tribes. That then excluded other groups that were within the confines or the boundaries of the Kingdom of Croats -- Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, as it eventually evolved. Were they equal -- I think they were equal in theory at the beginning of the period anyway. I don't know that they were really equal in -- in terms of the way they were treated during the course of the kingdom's history. And certainly after the dictatorship was proclaimed in 1929, you really couldn't say that the Croats and Slovenes were -- had equality with the Serbs in the kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Donia, I'm not speaking about the kingdom, I'm speaking about the state. The official name was the state of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes or Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. Do you know that the object was to unite with Serbia and that America recognised that unification? There's something wrong with the interpretation. Let's see what. It is my assertion that the territories which were once under Austro-Hungary, apart from Vojvodina that joined up with Serbia, the territories of today's Croatia, Slovenia, and today's Bosnia-Herzegovina, in using the principle of self-determination of peoples set in the American Congress and set out in Woodrow Wilson's 14 points, formed a state - a state, not a kingdom, a state - of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs which united with the Serbs, the kingdom came later. Now, do you know the existence of this state, the one that came before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of that state was the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. And it was -- it consisted of what had been the Kingdom of Serbia. It -- the Kingdom of Serbia had just completed a rather brutal annexation of Montenegro, which also then became a part of the kingdom, but with a proclamation of December 1. And then the other territories also became part of the kingdom with that proclamation. Now, there was certainly diplomatic, let's say, endorsement or validation of that proclamation and that creature, the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, in subsequent agreements as you've noted. But the act itself was something that took place in Belgrade and has to be seen, I think, as a -- it was certainly something that was done with the willing consent of all those people who claimed to represent those areas of the country at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Donia, it's an important link in the chain without which you can't understand the Yugoslav crisis. You don't know that before unification there was the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. It wasn't the kingdom, it wasn't called the kingdom, it was the territory west of the Drina, it was the Serb state west of the Drina composed of three peoples, the Slovenes, the Croats, and the Serbs, and if you don't know that, you are unable to understand the Yugoslav crisis. And it's a state in which they are constituent peoples, and if Yugoslavia was going to break down they wanted to have their own entity. So how can we continue this discussion if you don't know that fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which fact is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fact that a state existed, that the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, it was independent, without unification and before unification with the Serbs. It was formed and proclaimed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Donia doesn't know this key fact, and it's a key fact that the Serbs formed a state west of the Drina River and that together with the Slovenes and Croats they had a three-people state which united with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just put your question. You can give your evidence later on if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't think that that state ever existed before unification, you don't know about that? You're not conscious of any such state having existed; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you must be referring to something, but I have no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, these 14 points set out by Woodrow Wilson, I'd like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how relevant it is, but we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D243.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, you mention further on -- you mention the Bosnians, Bosniaks. Do you agree that we Bosnians, Serbs, and Croats and Bosnians -- Muslims by adopting this term, appropriated the term, and placed the monopoly over Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question's a little convoluted. I'm not exactly certain what you're asking when you said -- well, please, if you could ask the question again. I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was down to the interpretation. The Muslims recently changed their national name; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed their national name in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they took the name of Bosniak; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we, Serbs and Croats, are also Bosniaks, that Bosnia is our country too; so by the same token that's what we would be too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a distinction I think in both languages between "Bosnjak" and "Bosanac" or "Bosnjaci" and/or "Bosanci" in B/C/S and between Bosniak, which is a term that refers specifically to those people -- that people who used to be called the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnians, which refers to all citizens and/or residents of Bosnia, regardless of their national identity or ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But it is the usurpation of the name Bosniak, and the Muslims want to say by using Bosniak that Bosnia is theirs and that we're some guests there or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a -- some Bosniaks have attempted to do that. Most I think are of the view that the Bosniaks are now one of three primary nations living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with the Croats and Serbs, and would not accept that view of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they accepted that quite recently. Do you know what they were called during the Turkish occupation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call their identity hybrid. They -- there were a number of different names that were used to refer to them depending region where they were. I'm sure you have a particular word in mind here, but they were known as -- to some people they were called Turks, to some people they were called simply Muslims, and in Bosnia a lot of people were called Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Together with us, the Serbs and Croats. Then they were called undetermined, then they were called Muslims -- or rather, they were the constituent peoples. And now they're called Bosniaks, which the Serbs and Croats needn't like. But let's leave that aside. The B/C/S language, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, do you use it on a scientific scholarly basis or a political basis, this B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me it's a means of communication. I read it and speak it as best I can and use it to communicate. I don't know that I would say I use it on a political basis. I certainly use it in my scholarship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does B/C/S exist or is it in fact the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can do an interesting analysis of the language as it is used around here and probably not come up with an answer specifically, but I don't -- wouldn't agree that it is in fact the Serbian language. I think it is a -- B/C/S as it is referred to in this Tribunal and in some other international organisations probably is a blend of Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian language, particularly emphasizing their -- the common denominators among the three languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know when the Stokavian variant of the language came do -- do you know who Vuk Karadzic was? Let me ask you that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your last question, yes, I believe he was a distant relative of yours and -- or at least you look to his family for your family origins. And he was a Serbian literary figure at the beginning of the 19th century who collected folk tales and poetry and codified essentially the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he's a relative. My father's name was Vuk, his father's name was Stefan, so it's the same family. All Karadzics are related one way or another. But do you know that the Vienna Agreement -- Vuk allowed the Croatians to use the Stokavian language as being their language too and that the differentiation came later on and that the Serbs -- that this was stolen from the Serbs, and is language the cultural property of a people? Let me ask you that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a linguist, a linguistic expert. I can tell you that the languages don't get stolen, and the notion that it is a cultural property of a people I would really not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you think that Australia could say that it spoke Australian and not English or Brazil to say that it spoke Brazilian and not Portuguese? Do you think that that would be okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's well outside of my area of expertise, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 2 you said that in Yugoslavia national elections were never held on an ethnic, national basis, but that they were -- that the elections took place in the republics. Now, who prevented elections at the level of the nation of Yugoslavia according to the principle of one man/one vote? Did the Serbs prevent that from happening or was it separatists, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is they never came to an agreement. And so there were certainly people in all groups who favoured it, and I wouldn't reduce it to saying the Serbs favoured it and others opposed it. It just never got agreed upon. And just to clarify, we're talking now not about elections on an ethnic principle, but a single election for the entire SFRJ, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. A state nation or country-wide I think you said. Now, let me inform you that the Serbs were always while Yugoslavia existed in favour of the principle of one man/one vote, but that was unsuccessful; whereas, today the republics which separated are introducing the principle of one man/one vote to disenfranchise the Serb minority. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with either premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that now those republics are asking for the one man/one vote principle, whereas they failed to accept that while Yugoslavia was in existence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- that's just too simple a way of putting it. It's -- first of all reduces -- your original formulation reduces a very wide variety of viewpoints to the simple expression "the Serbs," and I guess you are speaking for the Serbs in that formulation. But I wouldn't agree that that was the case on such a universal basis at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not speaking on behalf of anyone now. Quite simply, one man/one vote at the level of Yugoslavia did not go through because the separatist republics would not allow it to go through, whereas now they are asking for one man/one vote. Now, who did we beat at the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990? I think this is on page 4 of this report of yours dealing with Sarajevo. You say: [In English] "A dozen or other parties that had been founded and registered in the preceding months." [Interpretation] Is it true that we beat the communists mostly and that there was a regime change?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the three nationalist parties together or separately did, in fact, defeat the two major non-nationalist parties, the socialist democrats and the reformists -- we're talking about Bosnia, if that's what we're referring to. And was there a regime change? Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Karadzic, I'm noting the time. Shall we adjourn for today? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two very quick matters to raise. First I wanted to inquire whether the Court had made a determination or confirmed that it can sit the extra time on the week of June 21st, our revised schedule is dependent to some extent on that -- well, to a large extent on that. And secondly, with respect to the recently filed application for certification and stay. I wanted to indicate that the Prosecution anticipated filing a response tomorrow if it's helpful for us to foreshadow that, I can do so at this point. But if the timing is satisfactory, we'll have that filed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I simply can't refrain from observing that which George Bernard Shaw said that "England and America are two countries separated by a common language."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.
